questions.question: When should you use `strings.Fields` instead of `strings.Split`?
questions.title: Fields versus Split
questions.direct_answer: Use `strings.Fields` to split text around runs of Unicode whitespace while discarding leading, trailing, and repeated empty gaps. Use `strings.Split` when one exact separator defines the format and empty fields may carry meaning. `Split` does not trim pieces, and splitting on an empty separator produces UTF-8 sequences for individual code points according to the package contract.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether tokenization rules and empty-field semantics are chosen from the real input format.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Parsing CSV with Split or deleting meaningful empty fields by switching to Fields.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why adjacent separators are data in one contract and noise in the other.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Fields` splits on one or more Unicode whitespace characters.
`Fields` discards leading, trailing, and repeated whitespace gaps.
`Split` preserves empty fields created by adjacent separators.
Choose by the input format, not by which output looks convenient once.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`strings.Fields` treats text as whitespace-separated words. It finds runs of characters for which Unicode defines whitespace and returns only non-empty fields. Leading and trailing whitespace disappear, and several spaces, tabs, or newlines between words behave as one boundary.

`strings.Split` treats one exact string as the delimiter. It preserves empty fields caused by adjacent or edge delimiters because those positions can be meaningful in a format. For example, splitting `"a,,c"` on comma returns `a`, an empty field, and `c`; using Fields would not parse commas at all.

For example, `Fields("  Go\tweb\nAPI  ")` returns three words without empty strings. `Split("  Go  ", " ")` returns empties for the repeated spaces. Calling `TrimSpace` before `Split` removes only the edge whitespace and still leaves internal empty fields.

I use Fields for human-entered whitespace-separated input and exact Split for delimited formats whose grammar really is that simple. CSV needs a CSV parser because quoting, escaping, and newlines make plain splitting incorrect. The key boundary is whether repeated delimiters are noise or actual empty values.

sections.title: Whitespace tokenization and delimiter parsing are different jobs
sections.content:
Fields applies a character classification and collapses runs. Split searches for exact separator occurrences and reports every segment between them. These contracts intentionally disagree on empty output because they model different data.

A format may outgrow both. CSV, shell syntax, URLs, and escaped key-value files have grammars that cannot be parsed reliably by one string separator. Use the format-specific package rather than layering trimming and replacement until one sample passes.

sections.title: How the two functions treat boundaries
sections.content:
| Input and operation | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Fields(" a  b ")` | `[a b]` | Whitespace runs collapse |
| `Split("a,,b", ",")` | `[a "" b]` | Empty middle field preserved |
| `Split(",a,", ",")` | `["" a ""]` | Edge fields preserved |
| `Fields(" \t ")` | `[]` | No non-whitespace field |

sections.title: Observe collapsed whitespace and preserved empty fields

questions.question: Which `strings` functions are useful for searching and trimming text?
questions.title: Searching, cutting, and trimming strings
questions.direct_answer: Use `strings.Contains` for substring presence, `HasPrefix` and `HasSuffix` for anchored checks, and `Index` when the byte position is needed. `Cut` splits once and reports whether a separator was found. `TrimSpace` removes surrounding Unicode whitespace, while `Trim`, `TrimPrefix`, and `TrimSuffix` have different cut-set or exact-boundary contracts and should not be treated as interchangeable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether search position, exact boundary, cut-set, whitespace, and missing-separator semantics remain distinct.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `Trim` as though its second argument were an exact prefix or suffix.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Index returns a byte offset and Cut preserves whether the separator was present.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `Contains` for presence and `Index` when its byte offset is needed.
Use `Cut` when splitting around the first separator and checking presence.
`Trim` removes a cut set of runes, not one exact substring.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `strings` package provides small operations with intentionally different contracts. `Contains` answers whether a substring occurs. `Index` returns the byte offset of its first occurrence or -1. `HasPrefix` and `HasSuffix` require the match at one boundary, so they communicate protocol markers and filename-style checks more clearly than a general search.

`Cut(text, separator)` is useful for one key-value boundary. It returns the text before, the text after, and a Boolean indicating whether the separator existed. That Boolean distinguishes `"mode="` from `"mode"`; blindly splitting and indexing can lose that difference or panic. Related `CutPrefix` and `CutSuffix` make exact optional boundary removal explicit.

Trimming needs equal care. `TrimSpace` removes leading and trailing Unicode whitespace. `Trim(text, "ab")` removes any leading or trailing `a` or `b` rune, not the exact substring `"ab"`. For an exact marker, use `TrimPrefix` or `TrimSuffix` and decide whether absence is acceptable.

For example, parsing `" mode = debug "` can trim the whole line, cut once on `=`, and trim both parts. This is suitable for a tiny controlled format. A real configuration grammar still needs validation for empty keys, duplicates, comments, and escapes. These functions make each text boundary visible but do not replace a parser.

sections.title: Select by position and failure information
sections.content:
Search functions differ on whether they return a Boolean, an offset, or separated pieces. Boundary functions differ on whether the target is an exact string, a set of runes, or Unicode whitespace. Matching the function to the rule reduces manual slicing and accidental panics.

Most returned indexes are byte offsets because Go strings are byte sequences. A match returned by a strings function is safe to use for slicing around that exact byte substring. It should not be relabeled as a rune position.

sections.title: Choose the exact operation
sections.content:
| Requirement | Function | Result detail |
|---|---|---|
| Is substring present? | `Contains` | Boolean |
| Where does it start? | `Index` | Byte offset or -1 |
| Remove exact leading marker | `TrimPrefix` / `CutPrefix` | New text; Cut also reports match |
| Split once and detect absence | `Cut` | Before, after, found |
| Remove surrounding whitespace | `TrimSpace` | Unicode whitespace removed |
| Remove any edge rune from a set | `Trim` | Cut-set semantics |

sections.title: Parse one explicit text boundary
sections.content:
```go
package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "strings"
)

func main() {
    line := strings.TrimSpace(" mode = debug ")
    key, value, found := strings.Cut(line, "=")
    fmt.Println(strings.TrimSpace(key), strings.TrimSpace(value), found)
    fmt.Println(strings.HasPrefix("go.mod", "go"), strings.Contains("gopher", "ph"))
}
```
The first output is `mode debug true`. Cut reports the separator instead of requiring a fragile length check.

questions.question: How should `strings.Builder` be used in Go?
questions.title: Using strings.Builder correctly
questions.direct_answer: Declare a zero-value `strings.Builder`, append text with `WriteString`, `WriteRune`, or `Write`, and call `String` for the result. Call `Grow` only when a useful size estimate exists. Do not copy a non-zero Builder; pass a pointer to helpers if needed. Use it for incremental text construction, while `strings.Join` is simpler when every piece already exists.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether Builder's zero value, growth, ownership, and alternative tools are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Copying a Builder after writing, or using one where Join expresses an already-collected slice more clearly.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the no-copy rule to buffer ownership and keep the Builder's lifetime local.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The zero value of `strings.Builder` is ready to use.
`Grow` may reduce reallocations when size is predictable.
A non-zero Builder must not be copied.
Use `Join` instead when a slice of final pieces already exists.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`strings.Builder` is a mutable construction object whose purpose is producing one string efficiently. Its zero value is ready, so ordinary code writes `var b strings.Builder`, appends pieces, and calls `b.String()`. Write methods return counts and, by current contract, a nil error, which lets Builder participate in formatting and writer-style helpers.

`Grow(n)` reserves space for at least another `n` bytes when the final size can be estimated. It is an optimization, not a correctness requirement, and a negative argument panics. `Reset` discards accumulated content. The most important usage rule is that a Builder must not be copied after the first write, because copies can share its internal buffer in unsupported ways.

For example, a helper can accept `*strings.Builder` and append one HTML-free label at a time. The caller keeps one owner. If helpers need independent results, each gets its own Builder. When all strings are already in a slice with one separator, `strings.Join` removes the manual loop and is usually clearer.

Builder is text-focused; `bytes.Buffer` is often more natural when code consumes or produces byte slices and uses reader methods. I do not put a reused Builder into a long-lived shared object without explicit synchronization. Construct locally, return the immutable string, and let the temporary builder disappear.

sections.title: One mutable owner produces one immutable result
sections.content:
Builder centralizes capacity and appends so growing text does not recreate every prefix at the source level. The zero-value design keeps local use simple. Pointer-passing maintains one owner when construction spans helpers.

The no-copy rule applies after use, so storing Builder as a casually copied struct field is risky. A short local lifetime also makes concurrency simple: each operation owns its builder, and only the resulting string crosses the boundary.

sections.title: Builder ownership lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[zero-value Builder] --> B[optional Grow]
  B --> C[WriteString or WriteRune]
  C --> C
  C --> D[String result]
  D --> E[immutable value returned]
  C -. never copy non-zero builder .-> F[unsupported alias]
```

sections.title: Keep one Builder owner across helpers
